claim: Wild cereal grain consumption among Early Holocene foragers of the Balkans predates the arrival of agriculture.
source: Wild cereal grain consumption among Early Holocene foragers of the Balkans predates the arrival of agriculture
evidence: This is the main claim of the manuscript, supported by starch grain and phytolith analyses of dental calculus and ground stone tools from Mesolithic individuals.

claim: Certain species of Poaceae (species of the genus Aegilops) were used since the Early Mesolithic.
source: Our results based on the study of dental calculus show that certain species of Poaceae (species of the genus Aegilops) were used since the Early Mesolithic, while GSTs exhibit traces of a developed grass grain processing technology.
evidence: Supported by starch grain analysis from dental calculus of Early Mesolithic individuals and comparison with modern reference collections.

claim: Ground stone tools exhibit traces of a developed grass grain processing technology.
source: Our results based on the study of dental calculus show that certain species of Poaceae (species of the genus Aegilops) were used since the Early Mesolithic, while GSTs exhibit traces of a developed grass grain processing technology.
evidence: Supported by functional analysis of ground stone tools showing use-wear and residues consistent with plant processing.

claim: The adoption of domesticated plants in this region after ~6500 cal BC might have been eased by the existing familiarity with wild cereals.
source: The adoption of domesticated plants in this region after ~6500 cal BC might have been eased by the existing familiarity with wild cereals.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the evidence of wild cereal use predating domesticated cereal introduction.

claim: Forager knowledge and consistent use of wild cereals are still debated and poorly documented outside of the assumed centers of domestication in southwestern Asia.
source: Forager knowledge and consistent use of wild cereals are still debated and poorly documented outside of the assumed centers of domestication in southwestern Asia (Kotsakis, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: In the Balkans some forms of intense gathering or incipient human management of local plant and animal species might have occurred before the full-blown transition to the Neolithic.
source: For some time, it has been claimed that in the Balkans some forms of intense gathering or incipient human management of local plant and animal species might have occurred before the full-blown transition to the Neolithic (Clarke, 1978; Halstead, 1996; Kotsakis, 2003; Kotzamani and Livarda, 2014; Srejović, 1988; ; y'Edynak and Fleisch, 1983), partly due to the region's geographical proximity to the Near East.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to existing literature.

claim: The hypothesis of a systematic use of wild grasses of the Poaceae family during the Mesolithic remains to be verified in this region.
source: However, the hypothesis of a systematic use of wild grasses of the Poaceae family (e.g., Aegilops spp.; Hordeum spp.) during the Mesolithic remains to be verified in this region.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: At Franchthi Cave in Greece, wild barley appears in the archaeobotanical record starting in the Late Upper Palaeolithic and throughout the Mesolithic.
source: Here, wild barley (Hordeum sp.) appears in the archaeobotanical record starting in the Late Upper Palaeolithic and throughout the Mesolithic, along with oat (Avena sp.), pulses (Lens sp. Mill.), bitter vetch (Vicia ervilia (L.) Willd.), almond (Prunus amygdalus Batscht), and terebinth (Pistacia cf. lentiscus L.) (Hansen, 1991; Van Andel et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeobotanical studies.

claim: At Vlakno Cave in Croatia, starch granules of wild species of barley and oat were found in the dental calculus of a Mesolithic forager individual dating to the late eight millennium cal BC.
source: More recently, at Vlakno Cave in Croatia, starch granules of a wild species of barley (Hordeum spp.), along with those of oat (Avena spp.), were found in the dental calculus of a Mesolithic forager individual, dating to the late eight millennium cal BC burial (Cristiani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cereal-type pollen increased in the Late Mesolithic across Europe.
source: Besides this type of evidence, data about the increase of cereal-type pollen in the Late Mesolithic (LM) come from palynological spectra from across Europe.
evidence: This claim is based on palynological evidence from multiple sites.

claim: The presence of Cerealia-type pollens in pollen spectra could be highly indicative of anthropic origin of disturbance phases.
source: Due to low dispersal rates of cereal-type pollen grains as well as Cerealia-type pollens, their very presence in pollen spectra could be highly indicative of anthropic origin of disturbance phases (Edwards, 1989), and could be interpreted as forest clearances.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and inference from pollen dispersal characteristics.

claim: There is growing evidence of the active role of hunter-gatherers in shaping their landscape ecologies, including plant management.
source: Moreover, far from seeing foragers as passive recipients of novelties arriving from Neolithic groups at the time of agricultural transitions, there is now growing evidence of the active role of hunter–gatherers in shaping their landscape ecologies, including plant management, and manipulation of ecosystems through niche constructing (Lombardo et al., 2020; Rowley-Conwy and Layton, 2011; Smith, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature on hunter-gatherer ecology.

claim: The Danube Gorges area is one of the best researched areas of Europe regarding the Mesolithic–Neolithic transition period.
source: This is one of the best researched areas of Europe regarding the Mesolithic–Neolithic transition period with more than 20 sites spanning the duration of the Epipalaeolithic through to the Mesolithic and EN (~13,000–5500 cal BC) (Bonsall, 2008; Borić, 2011; Borić, 2016; Radovanović, 1996; Srejović, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeological literature on the region.

claim: Open-air sites in the Danube Gorges began appearing with the start of the Holocene warming on river terrace promontories.
source: Open-air sites began appearing in the archaeological record with the start of the Holocene warming on river terrace promontories in the vicinity of strong whirlpools, narrows, and rapids of the Danube, which facilitated intense fishing operations (Borić, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to archaeological evidence.

claim: From the Early Mesolithic onwards, sites in the Danube Gorges became places for continuous interment of the dead.
source: From the Early Mesolithic (EM) onwards, these sites became places for a continuous interment of the dead (Borić, 2016; Borić et al., 2014; Radovanović, 1996), thus creating a substantial mortuary record, which is in the excess of 500 individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeological evidence.

claim: Fishing seems to have remained one of the main subsistence foci throughout the Holocene in the Danube Gorges.
source: Fishing seems to have remained one of the main subsistence foci throughout the Holocene, with a possible intensification during the LM (~7300–6200 cal BC), the period that saw an intense inhabitation of the area, with recognizable features in the archaeological record, such as stone-lined rectangular hearths and abundant primary burials placed as extended inhumations parallel with the Danube River.
evidence: This claim is based on archaeological evidence and inference from site features.

claim: Between ~6200 and 5900 cal BC, local Mesolithic foragers came into contact with the first Neolithic groups appearing in the Danube Gorges region.
source: Between ~6200 and 5900 cal BC, there are clearest indications based on both material culture associations and isotope and genomic data (Borić and Price, 2013; Mathieson et al., 2018) that the local Mesolithic foragers came into contact with the first Neolithic groups appearing in this region, and who likely founded several new sites in this area, especially in the downstream part of the region.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to isotope and genomic studies.

claim: After ~5900 cal BC, the forager cultural specificity was lost in the Danube Gorges area.
source: After ~5900 cal BC, it seems that the forager cultural specificity was lost and that various sites remained to be used as typical EN Starčevo culture villages up until ~5500 cal BC, when most of the previously used locales were abandoned.
evidence: This claim is based on archaeological evidence and inference from material culture changes.

claim: Nonflaked tools such as pestles, grinders, crushers, and anvils have been associated with fruit, seed, and nut processing in early prehistoric and ethnographic contexts.
source: Nonflaked tools such as pestles, grinders, crushers, and anvils have recently been associated with fruit, seed, and nut processing in early prehistoric and ethnographic contexts (de Beaune, 2004; Dubreuil and Nadel, 2015; Hamon et al., 2021; Pardoe et al., 2019; Wright, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeological and ethnographic studies.

claim: Ground stone tools are primarily documented from the Late Mesolithic onwards in the Danube Gorges region.
source: However, this category of artifacts is primarily documented from the LM onwards and only sporadically associated with earlier periods in the region of the Danube Gorges (Antonović, 2006; Borić et al., 2014; Srejović and Letica, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeological evidence.

claim: Recent carpological analyses indicated a relatively wide spectrum of wild resources available to local Mesolithic foragers in the Danube Gorges.
source: Despite a generally poor preservation of plant remains due to taphonomic issues, recent carpological analyses indicated a relatively wide spectrum of wild resources available to the local Mesolithic foragers. These included drupes, fruits, and berries (Marinova et al., 2013), among which cornelian cherry (Cornus mas L.), hazelnut (Corylus avellana L.), and elderberry (Sambucus nigra L.) were the most frequent taxa (Filipović et al., 2010; Marinova et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to carpological studies.

claim: Molecular record of Corylus avellana and Sambucus nigra was found preserved in the dental calculus of two Late Mesolithic individuals from Vlasac.
source: Molecular record of C. avellana and S. nigra was also found preserved in the dental calculus of two LM individuals from Vlasac, which underwent metagenomic analysis (Ottoni et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a metagenomic study.

claim: At the site of Vlasac, presumed human palaeofeces contained pollen of Amaranthaceae and Cerealia.
source: Moreover, in the study region of the Danube Gorges, at the site of Vlasac, presumed human palaeofeces contained pollen of Amaranthaceae and Cerealia (Cârciumaru, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a palynological study.

claim: Evidence from the Mesolithic levels at the site of Icoana has suggested local cereal cultivation.
source: Evidence from the Mesolithic levels at the site of Icoana, located in the same region, has suggested local cereal cultivation (Cârciumaru, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to archaeological evidence.

claim: Starch granules identified in dental calculus within a sample of 12 individuals provided evidence for the consumption of domesticated cereals at the site of Vlasac during the Late Mesolithic.
source: More recently, starch granules identified in dental calculus within a sample of 12 individuals provided evidence for the consumption of domesticated cereals at the site of Vlasac during the LM (Cristiani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Starch granules were almost ubiquitous in the analyzed individuals.
source: Starch granules were almost ubiquitous in the analyzed individuals and many of them were found still in part associated with dental calculus remains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Six morphotypes of starch granules have been retrieved in this study.
source: Six morphotypes have been retrieved in this study (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in tables.

claim: Type I starch granules are characterized by size, shape, morphology, and bimodal distribution encountered in Europe only in the members of the plant tribe Triticeae.
source: Size, shape, morphology, and bimodal distribution that characterize granules of this type are encountered in Europe only in the members of the plant tribe Triticeae (Poaceae family) and considered diagnostic features for taxonomic identification (Henry and Piperno, 2008; Stoddard, 1999; Yang and Perry, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on starch grain identification.

claim: A unimodal starch granule size distribution is common in the species of the genus Aegilops of the Triticeae tribe.
source: Several studies (Howard et al., 2011; Stoddard and Sarker, 2000) suggested that this characteristic is common in the species of the genus Aegilops of the Triticeae tribe and can be attributed to both environment (Blumenthal et al., 1995; Blumenthal et al., 1994) and genetics (Stoddard and Sarker, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on starch granule distribution.

claim: Type I starch granules were documented in most of the analyzed Mesolithic individuals.
source: Type I (Ia and Ib) is very common in the analyzed samples (Table 2), as already emphasized in our earlier study albeit in different quantities (Cristiani et al., 2016). These starch granules were documented, often lodged in the amyloplast, in most of the analyzed Mesolithic individuals (5 for EM, 16 for LM, 5 for M/N), and in 5 EN individuals of our population (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: A-Type granules recovered in Early Mesolithic and most of the Late Mesolithic individuals were very large, mostly with a clear, round shape, central hilum, and high density of deep lamellae.
source: A-Type granules recovered in EM and most of the LM individuals were very large, mostly with a clear, round shape, central hilum, and high density of deep lamellae mainly concentrated in the mesial part of the granules.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: The characteristics of A-Type granules are consistent with most species of the Triticeae tribe.
source: Based on literature (Henry et al., 2011; Yang and Perry, 2013) and our extensive experimental and statistical results on modern botanical collection (Table 4; Table 5; Figures 6, 7 and 9), we confirm that these characteristics are consistent with A-Type granules of most species of the Triticeae tribe.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: Subtype Ia starch granules are characterized by a combination of oval A-Type granules and uniformly small, round B-Type granules.
source: A few LM and M/N individuals (e.g., HV11 and 16, H53, 64.x11, H327, H232) yielded a combination of oval A-Type granules and uniformly small, round B-Type granules (Figure 4m).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Subtype Ia pattern is a recognizable feature of the domestic species of the tribe Triticeae.
source: Our previous claims that this pattern is a recognizable feature of the domestic species of the tribe Triticeae (e.g., Triticum spp./Hordeum spp.) (Figure 6 and 9; Cristiani et al., 2016) are now further supported by a new morphometric analysis of both domestic and wild Triticeae species (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analysis and comparison with previous work.

claim: In Early Neolithic individuals, lenticular and oval/suboval A-Type granules with equatorial groove are always associated with very small and uniformly shaped B-Type granules.
source: Moreover, in the same individuals, A-Type granules could show cratered appearance (Figure 4). Similarly, in the EN individuals, lenticular and oval/suboval A-Type granules with equatorial groove and, an often visible, cratered surface are always associated with very small and uniformly shaped B-Type granules.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Type A granules appear damaged in few Early Neolithic individuals, which may be linked to enzymatic digestion or plant food processing.
source: Type A granules appear damaged in few EN individuals, which may be linked to enzymatic digestion (salivary amylase) although plant food processing could also result in starch damage based on experimental results (Soto et al., 2019; Zupancich et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation and citations to experimental studies.

claim: Subtype Ib starch granules are characterized by significant unevenness in granule dimensions and shape.
source: Significant unevenness in granule dimensions and shape was recorded in the EM and most of the LM individuals (e.g., PAD9 and VL45). Granules in this subtype are dimensionally variable and their shapes can range from round to oval (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Type II starch granules consist of large aggregates as well as clustered polyhedral/irregular granules.
source: Starch granules attributed to this type consist of large aggregates as well as clustered polyhedral/irregular granules (main axis ranging from 5 to 15 μm). They were retrieved from 10 individuals (2 EM, 11 LM, 2 M/N, and 3 EN) (Table 2; Figure 4g).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Type II starch granules were grouped in the tribe Aveneae/Poeae based on large aggregates found mostly in the genus Avena.
source: The identification of archaeological specimens is based on published records (Mariotti Lippi et al., 2015) and our experimental reference (Avena barbata L., A. strigosa Schreb., and A. fatua L.) (Figure 7). Granules of this morphotype were grouped in the tribe Aveneae/Poeae based on the fact that such large aggregates are found mostly in the genus Avena L. (oat), which is very common in the region.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and experimental reference collection.

claim: Type III starch granules are characterized by a polyhedral to subpolyhedral 3D morphology, a central hilum, and fine cracks.
source: Starch granules attributed to this type are characterized by a polyhedral to subpolyhedral 3D morphology, a central hilum, and fine cracks. They were recovered in 16 individuals (5 for EM, 16 for LM, 2 for M/N, and 1 for EN) (Table 2; Figure 4c and Figure 5b, c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Type III starch granules are consistent with starch granules of the tribe Paniceae of the grass family Poaceae.
source: These features are consistent with starch granules of the tribe Paniceae of the grass family Poaceae and very well known in ancient starch research (Madella et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on starch grain identification.

claim: Type III starch granules fall within the size range found in several species of Setaria spp., Panicum spp., and Echinochloa spp.
source: In our sample, starch granules assigned to type III reach 21 μm of maximum width, which falls within the size range found in several species of Setaria spp., Panicum spp., and Echinochloa spp. (Lucarini et al., 2016; Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and comparison with reference collection.

claim: Type IV starch granules are identified in 10 individuals.
source: Starch granules of this type are identified in 10 individuals (2 EM, 8 LM, 1 M/N, and 2 EN) and are recovered above 6 granules per specimen, with the exception of the only EN individual (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Type IV starch granules are diagnostic of starch granules included in the species of the plant family Fabaceae.
source: Diagnostic morphological characteristics for Type IV granules are known in ancient starch research and include a reniform shape in 3D, a collapsed/sunken hilum forming a deep fissure along almost the entire granule, and a size ranging between 12 and 35 μm (Henry et al., 2011). Small cracks were observed departing from such hilum and were very evident under cross-polarized light. In most cases the extinction cross was very bright and showed several lateral arms diverging from the hilum in correspondence with the cracks (Figure 4h). Moreover, lamellae were visible toward the outer part of the granules. All these features are very peculiar and diagnostic of starch granules included in the species of the plant family Fabaceae (Henry et al., 2011), which is mostly known for its several edible domesticated species of legumes (e.g., Lens culinaris Medikus, Vicia faba L., and Pisum sativum L.), but also has a number of wild edible such as vetches (Vicia spp.).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on starch grain identification.

claim: Type V starch granules have been identified in eight individuals.
source: Few starch granules attributed to this type have been identified in eight individuals (2 EM, 5LM, nd 1MN) (Figures 4d and 5a; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Type V starch granules were found to have a very close visual match with the starch found in acorns of oaks (Quercus spp.).
source: This type was found to have a very close visual match with the starch found in acorns of oaks (Quercus spp.), a Fagaceae member and well known in ancient starch research (Liu et al., 2015; Figure 7i, j).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and comparison with reference collection.

claim: Type VI starch granules have been identified in two individuals.
source: Granules ascribed to this type have been identified in two individuals (1 LM and 1 M/N) (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Type VI starch granules are assigned to species of the family Cornaceae (e.g., Cornus mas).
source: Zarrillo and Kooyman, 2017 consider these morphological features diagnostic of some species of drupes and berries. In our sample, starch granules of this morphotype can reach 12 μm of maximum width, which is beyond species of berries and drupes in the Rosaceae family known in literature (Zarrillo and Kooyman, 2017) and in our modern reference (e.g., Prunus spinosa L.). Based on our experimental record, we assign type VI to species of the family Cornaceae (e.g., C. mas) (Figure 7), the remains of which are documented at Vlasac (Filipović et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation, experimental reference, and archaeological evidence.

claim: 42 phytoliths were retrieved in 24 individuals.
source: In addition to starch granules, 42 phytoliths were retrieved in 24 individuals (EM = 4; LM = 13; MN = 2; N = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Mostly short cells, commonly produced in leaves, stems and inflorescences, were identified and attributed to Pooid grasses.
source: Mostly, short cells, commonly produced in leaves, stems and inflorescences, were identified and attributed to Pooid grasses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Multicellular structures of long cells were identified in Mesolithic individuals.
source: Multicellular structures of long cells were identified in Mesolithic individuals (HV25/26, VL70, VL79, and U222) (Figure 4j and k; Figure 5m).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Single or multicellular dendritic structures were identified in Neolithic individuals.
source: Single or multicellular dendritic structures were also identified in Neolithic individuals (VEL-2D and Gârleşti) (Figure 4w, x).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Dendritic phytoliths in local forager dental calculus are likely related to plant consumption.
source: Yet, the presence of few dendritic phytoliths in local forager dental calculus is likely related to plant consumption, as such microremains have experimentally been associated with mechanical destruction of husks and culms of Pooids by grinding (Portillo and Albert, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental studies and inference.

claim: Diagnostic use-wear and residues are identified on 44 ground stone tools from the site of Vlasac.
source: Diagnostic use-wear and residues are identified on 44 GSTs from the site of Vlasac.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: A total of 17 ground stone tools have surfaces bearing functional areas positively associated with plant food processing.
source: Within the tools displaying diagnostic use-wear, a total of 17 GSTs have surfaces bearing functional areas positively associated with plant food processing (Table 3; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: The combination of use-wear and macroresidues on ground stone tools are commonly associated with crushing and grinding grass grains and/or fruits.
source: The aforementioned combination of use-wear and macroresidues are commonly associated with GSTs used as handstones for crushing and grinding grass grains and/or fruits, such as hazelnuts and/or acorns in our experimental record (Cristiani and Zupancich, 2020; Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: A total of 137 starch granules have been retrieved from the surfaces of the ground stone tools.
source: A total of 137 starch granules have been retrieved from the surfaces of the GSTs characterized by plant-related functional microscopic features.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Residues and use-wear identified on ground stone tools from Late Mesolithic Vlasac show the existence of a plant food processing technology aimed at preparing a coarse-grained flour.
source: In sum, several hundreds of starch granules and phytoliths of grass grains of the Triticeae tribe have been identified in the analyzed dental calculus of the Mesolithic population in the Danube Gorges. In addition, residues and use-wear identified on GSTs from LM Vlasac show the existence of a plant food processing technology during this period aimed at preparing a coarse-grained flour through a combination of pounding and grinding gestures (Table 3; Figure 3 and Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study and inference from use-wear patterns.

claim: The consumption of partially processed grains is corroborated by the presence of starch granules still lodged in their amyloplast on Mesolithic ground stone tools and dental calculus.
source: The conclusion about the consumption of partially processed grains is corroborated by the presence of starch granules still lodged in their amyloplast on Mesolithic GSTs and dental calculus, as suggested in our previous study (Cristiani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study and citation to previous work.

claim: A-Type granules in Early Neolithic dental calculus exhibit a damage pattern observed when producing fine-grained flour experimentally only through prolonged bidirectional grinding.
source: Interestingly, A-Type granules in EN dental calculus are generally retrieved singularly and exhibit a damage pattern observed when producing fine-grained flour experimentally only through prolonged bidirectional grinding (Dietrich et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental studies and comparison with archaeological data.

claim: The pattern of bidirectional grinding is not documented on the examined Late Mesolithic ground stone tools from Vlasac.
source: The pattern of bidirectional grinding is not documented on the examined LM GST from Vlasac, suggesting the existence of two different grain processing modalities typical of respective Mesolithic and Neolithic cultural traditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study and inference about cultural differences.

claim: Wild pulses and bitter vetch were used as foodstuffs for the Mesolithic inhabitants of Franchthi Cave.
source: While a secure identification to species or genus was not possible in our samples, we know that wild pulses (Lens sp. Mill.) and bitter vetch (V. ervilia (L.) Willd.) were used as foodstuffs for the Mesolithic inhabitants of Franchthi Cave (Asouti et al., 2018; Van Andel et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeobotanical studies.

claim: Wild legumes are well represented at Uzzo Cave, Italy, along with other arboreal fruits, acorns, and wild grapes.
source: Further evidence for a pre-Neolithic consumption of the species of the tribe Fabeae comes from Uzzo Cave, Italy, where wild legumes (Lathyrus sp. L., Pisum sp. L.) are well represented along with other arboreal fruits (Arbutus unedo L.), acorns (Quercus sp. L.), and wild grapes (Vitis vinifera subsp. sylvestris L.) (Costantini, 1989), as well as from the site of Barma Abeurador in southern France (Vaquer et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeobotanical studies.

claim: Fragments of acorns were found at several Mesolithic sites across Europe and in the Danube Gorges region.
source: Fragments of acorns were found at several Mesolithic sites across Europe (Holden et al., 1995; Kubiak-Martens, 1999) and in the investigated region (Mason, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeobotanical studies.

claim: Cornelian cherries are the most recurrent macroremains at Vlasac and are documented across Europe as a Mesolithic source of food and medicine.
source: Cornelian cherries are the most recurrent macroremains at Vlasac and are documented across Europe as a Mesolithic source of food and medicine (Divišová and Šída, 2015; Filipović et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeobotanical studies.

claim: Various fruits commonly referred to as 'cherries' and/or 'berries' are particularly well documented among Native American groups.
source: Ethnographically, various fruits commonly referred to as 'cherries' and/or 'berries' are particularly well documented among Native American groups (Siegfried, 1994; Zarrillo and Kooyman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ethnographic studies.

claim: Woodland Cree people used to mix berries and cherries with fish eggs and meat.
source: Interestingly, Woodland Cree people used to mix berries and cherries with fish eggs (Siegfried, 1994) and meat (Lowie, 1922).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ethnographic studies.

claim: Long-lasting interactions with edible grains documented in the Balkans since the end of the Pleistocene might have allowed enough time for specific eating habits, tastes, and 'cultural valuation' to develop.
source: We conclude that the long-lasting interactions with edible grains (but also wild pulses), documented in the Balkans since the end of the Pleistocene might have allowed enough time for specific eating habits, tastes, and 'cultural valuation' (Hastorf and Foxhall, 2017) to develop.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the evidence presented and citation to literature on food culture.

claim: Shared knowledge about specific plant resources effectively predates the introduction of agriculture in Europe.
source: Such a shared knowledge about specific plant resources effectively predates the introduction of agriculture in Europe, and might have eventually eased the introduction of domesticated species starting from the second half of the seventh millennium BC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evidence presented in the study.

claim: The examined collection of teeth contained a total of 155 specimens, of which 60 individuals had sufficiently preserved calculi for further analyses.
source: The examined collection of the teeth previously studied for strontium isotopes (Borić and Price, 2013) from five sites in the Danube Gorges area and the site of Gârleşti from the region of Oltenia in Romania and additionally collected teeth from the sites of the Velesnica and the 2006–2009 excavations at Vlasac contained a total of 155 specimens. Of these, a total of 60 individuals had sufficiently preserved calculi for further analyses (Table 1): 13 individuals date to the EM, 29 to the LM, 9 to the Mesolithic–Neolithic transition phase (M/N), and 8 to the EN.
evidence: This claim describes the sample size and composition of the study.

claim: 101 sandstone ground stone tools of the 131 implements found at the site of Vlasac were analyzed.
source: In order to corroborate data obtained through dental calculus analysis, we also analyzed 101 sandstone GSTs of the 131 implements found at the site of Vlasac during the 1970–1971 excavations and chronologically attributed to the LM (Borić et al., 2014; Srejović and Letica, 1978).
evidence: This claim describes the sample of ground stone tools analyzed in the study.

claim: The site of Vlasac yielded the richest Mesolithic assemblage of nonflaked stone tools recovered so far in the region.
source: This site yielded the richest Mesolithic assemblage of nonflaked stone tools recovered so far in the region (Antonović, 2006; Borić et al., 2014; Srejović and Letica, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeological literature.

claim: Decontamination and extraction procedures were conducted in dedicated clean spaces under strict environmental monitoring.
source: Decontamination and the extraction procedures for microdebris were conducted in dedicated clean spaces not connected to modern botanical work and under strict environmental monitoring of the DANTE laboratory of Sapienza University of Rome (IT), the BioArch laboratory at University of York (UK), and the aDNA facility of the University of Vienna (Austria). In all of these facilities, strict contamination rules were followed.
evidence: This describes the methodological procedures to prevent contamination.

claim: Control samples from clean working tables and dust traps were collected and analyzed for comparative purposes to prevent modern contamination.
source: Furthermore, control samples from the clean working tables and dust traps were collected and analyzed for comparative purposes in order to prevent any type of modern contamination in these laboratories – this is a practice routinely done in our laboratories, even at times where no archaeological analysis occur, to allow a better understanding of the flow of contaminations through seasons.
evidence: This describes the methodological procedures to monitor contamination.

claim: Synthetic and plant fibers and hairs, fungal spores and hyphae, palm and conifer pollens, insects' debris were detected in control samples.
source: Our results based on this procedure show that synthetic and plant fibers and hairs, fungal spores and hyphae, palm and conifer pollens, insects' debris; maize starch granules were detected twice while unidentified small starch granules were very rare; phytoliths and starch granules belonging to species of the Triticeae tribe were never recovered (Figure 10).
evidence: This describes the results of contamination monitoring.

claim: Phytoliths and starch granules belonging to species of the Triticeae tribe were never recovered in control samples.
source: Our results based on this procedure show that synthetic and plant fibers and hairs, fungal spores and hyphae, palm and conifer pollens, insects' debris; maize starch granules were detected twice while unidentified small starch granules were very rare; phytoliths and starch granules belonging to species of the Triticeae tribe were never recovered (Figure 10).
evidence: This describes the results of contamination monitoring, supporting the authenticity of archaeological finds.

claim: A modern reference collection of 300 plants native to the Balkans, the Mediterranean region, and Europe was used for comparison.
source: A modern reference collection of 300 plants native to the Balkans, the Mediterranean region, and Europe was used as a comparison, along with published literature, for the identification of archaeological starch granules.
evidence: This describes the reference materials used for identification.

claim: Caryopses from 11 Aegilops species, 1 Hordeum species, and 2 Triticum species grown in the central Balkans were collected for morphometric analysis.
source: Caryopses from 11 Aegilops species (A. triuncialis, A. comosa, A. crassa, A. cylindrica, A. geniculata, A. neglecta, A. speltoides tauschii, A. peregrina, A. triuncialis, A. uniaristata, and A. ventricosa), 1 Hordeum species (Hordeum vulgare distichon), and 2 Triticum species (Triticum monococcum and T. dicoccum) grown in the central Balkans were collected.
evidence: This describes the materials used for morphometric analysis.

claim: Aegilops sp. starch granules show a larger size distribution than Hordeum sp. and Triticum sp.
source: In general, the present experimental analysis revealed that Aegilops sp. starch granules show a larger size distribution than Hordeum sp. and Triticum sp. (Figures 6 and 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphometric analysis presented in the study.

claim: Aegilops spp. starch measurements are significantly different from those obtained for Hordeum sp. and Triticum sp.
source: This evidence is also supported by the pairwise Wilcoxon test, which highlights that Aegilops spp. starch measurements are significantly different from those obtained for Hordeum sp. and Triticum sp. counts (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in the study.

claim: Starch granules of oat caryopses have been processed as foodstuff during the Upper Palaeolithic at Paglicci Cave in southern Italy.
source: Very abundant in temperate ecosystems, oat caryopses have been processed as foodstuff already during the Upper Palaeolithic at Paglicci Cave, in the south of Italy (Mariotti Lippi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Oat starch granules have been documented in the dental calculus of a Late Mesolithic individual from Vlakno Cave in the Eastern Adriatic region.
source: They have also been documented in the dental calculus of the aforementioned LM individual from Vlakno Cave in the Eastern Adriatic region (Cristiani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The concentration of semiopen aggregates of Aveneae starch sustains the hypothesis of coarse processing of the seeds during the Mesolithic.
source: In our case study, exceptionally well-preserved aggregates of Aveneae have been identified in dental calculus only. The concentration of semiopen aggregates (Figures 4g, 5k and u) sustains the hypothesis of a coarse processing of the seeds during the Mesolithic, already suggested for other grass grain taxa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preservation state of starch granules.

claim: No evidence of millet consumption has been ascertained on the basis of stable isotope analysis in the Danube Gorges.
source: Our results confirm previous conclusions about the use of grasses of the tribe Paniceae by the LM foragers (Cristiani et al., 2016), while extending the consumption of this general types of millets to EM foragers too. However, no evidence of this food has been ascertained on the basis of stable isotope analysis (Borić et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to isotope studies.

claim: A great variety of species of C4 plants belonging to the tribe Paniceae and the tribe Andropogoneae grow well nearby water environments and slow-flowing waters.
source: We stress that a great variety of species of C4 plants belonging to the tribe Paniceae and the tribe Andropogoneae (e.g., species of plants of the genera Setaria Beauv. and Echinochloa P. Beauv.) grow well nearby water environments and slow-flowing waters, and it is very likely that a mixture of species from such genera might have contributed to the Mesolithic diet.
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological knowledge of plant distributions.

claim: The presence of Paniceae and Andropogoneae tribes, combined with evidence of feather barbule fragments from aquatic birds, points to familiarity with resources from riverine environments other than fish.
source: The presence of Paniceae and the Andropogoneae tribes, combined with the evidence of several feather barbule fragments from aquatic birds, clearly point to a familiarity with resources from riverine environments other than fish.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of plant and animal remains.

claim: Adoption of previously unknown plant foods is often facilitated by local foods that in shape and taste resemble the new arrivals.
source: Adoption of previously unknown plant foods is often facilitated by those local foods that in shape and taste resemble the new arrivals (Livarda, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on food adoption.

claim: Incipient management practices on certain wild plant taxa have been documented among nonagricultural societies.
source: Incipient management practices on certain wild plant taxa have been documented among nonagricultural societies for environmental and/or cultural reasons, for protecting or promoting the relative abundance of a species, or for reducing the energy involved in its harvesting (Fuller et al., 2011; Smith, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on plant management.

claim: A recent study of dental calculus from the Danube Gorges area concluded that domesticated cereals started to be used in this region only with the start of the Neolithic.
source: Another recent study of dental calculus from the Danube Gorges area has reached a conclusion that domesticated cereals started to be used in this region only with the start of the Neolithic (Jovanović et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Jovanović et al., 2021b disregard the evidence of Aegilops consumption during the Early Mesolithic as an 'implausible pattern'.
source: In the same study, the individuals dated to the EM exhibit a high occurrence of starch granules, which we have shown to be compatible with a variety of wild species of the Triticeae tribe (e.g., genus Aegilops). Jovanović et al., 2021b disregard the evidence of Aegilops consumption during the EM as an 'implausible pattern'.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The results of this study are in opposition to the conclusions of Jovanović et al., 2021b.
source: However, our results based on the combination of a robust sample of analyzed individuals, GSTs, and experimental data are in opposition to the conclusions of the mentioned study.
evidence: This is a statement of disagreement with another study based on the current evidence.

claim: Most prehistoric forager groups might have had regular access to plant nutrients and some sort of dependency on specific plants.
source: Most of prehistoric forager groups might have had regular access to plant nutrients and some sort of dependency on specific plants (Fuller et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on forager subsistence.

claim: Local foragers consumed oat, legumes, minor millet species, acorns, and Cornelian cherries besides wild grasses.
source: Accordingly, in our analysis of dental calculus and GSTs, we have shown that besides wild grasses, local foragers consumed oat, legumes, minor millet species of the genus Echinochloa and/or Setaria known as 'forgotten millets' (Madella et al., 2013; Weber and Fuller, 2008), acorns, and Cornelian cherries (Figure 4; Table 1 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Between 200 and 450 indigenous European edible plants are found concentrated in wetland habitats.
source: Furthermore, between 200 and 450 indigenous European edible plants (grass seeds, nuts, fruits, roots, tubers, and pulses) are found concentrated in wetland (coastal, lacustrine, and riparian) habitats (Clarke, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on European plant resources.

claim: Hundreds of Mesolithic sites across Europe have yielded remains of hazelnuts, acorns, water-chestnuts, and other plant remains.
source: Despite preservation and recovery problems, hundreds of Mesolithic sites across Europe have yielded the remains of hazelnuts, acorns, water-chestnuts, and other remains (Zvelebil, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a synthesis of European Mesolithic plant use.

claim: The chronological framework suggests that interest in and familiarity with various species of wild grasses of the Triticeae tribe dates back to at least ∼9500 cal BC.
source: The chronological framework of the analyzed sample suggests that this interest in and familiarity with various species of wild grasses of the Triticeae tribe (namely grass grains of the genus Aegilops) dates back to at least ∼9500 cal BC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dating of samples with Triticeae starch granules.

claim: Macrobotanical remains belonging to the genus Aegilops have not been recovered in Mesolithic and Early Neolithic sites in the central Balkans.
source: Macrobotanical remains belonging to this genus have not been recovered in Mesolithic and EN sites in the central Balkans (Cristiani et al., 2016: 10301).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The absence of Aegilops in the archaeobotanical record could be the result of taphonomic and recovery problems.
source: However, such absence in the archaeobotanical record could be the result of a host of taphonomic and recovery problems and should not be used to exclude the use of this genus during the Mesolithic (contra Cristiani et al., 2016: 4).
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of archaeobotanical evidence.

claim: Three Late Mesolithic individuals from Vlasac and two presumed Early Neolithic individuals from Lepenski Vir exhibit starches consistent with domesticated cereal species.
source: We have previously argued that three LM individuals from the site of Vlasac dated to the mid-seventh millennium cal BC (H53, 64.x11, and H232), as well as two presumed EN individuals from Lepenski Vir (8 and 20) exhibit starches consistent with domesticated cereal species, such as Triticum monococcum L. (einkorn wheat), Triticum dicoccum L. (emmer wheat), and/or Hordeum distichon L. (barley) (Cristiani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The bimodal pattern of starch granules distribution is commonly attributed to domestic species and absent in most wild species of the genus Aegilops.
source: This observation was based on the bimodal pattern of starch granules distribution, commonly attributed to domestic species and absent in most of the wild species of the genus Aegilops (Howard et al., 2011; Stoddard, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on starch grain distributions.

claim: Burial 20 from Lepenski Vir has recently been directly AMS-dated to the Early Mesolithic.
source: However, burial 20 from Lepenski Vir, previously published as dating to the EN, has recently been directly AMS-dated to the EM (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dating data presented in the study.

claim: The small number of starch granules found in burial 20 might have affected the visibility of potential variation in A-Type vs. B-Type population.
source: At the face of the current evidence, we explain this inconsistency in our results by arguing that the admittedly small number of starch granules found in this archaeological specimen might have affected the visibility of the potential variation in A-Type vs. B-Type population.
evidence: This is an inference to explain an inconsistency in the data.

claim: A large variability of starch granule distributions among different species of the Triticeae tribe has been acknowledged in the literature.
source: Moreover, a large variability of starch granule distributions among different species of the Triticeae tribe has been acknowledged in the literature (Henry and Piperno, 2008; Yang and Perry, 2013) and supported by our experimental reference (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: Fluctuations in environmental and growing conditions have been recognised as relevant factors affecting starch granule size distribution.
source: Furthermore, fluctuations in environmental and growing conditions have also been recognised as relevant factors affecting starch granule size distribution (Stoddard, 1999; Stoddard and Sarker, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on starch grain variability.

claim: It remains unclear to what extent plant foods contributed to the diet of the Danube Gorges foragers.
source: For the moment, it remains unclear to what extent plant foods, and species of the Poaceae family, contributed to the diet of the Danube Gorges foragers, and it is equally difficult to be more specific about the range of activities involved in their acquisition prior to processing and consumption – from sporadic collecting of wild grasses to forest clearances, or some form of indigenous system of plant management.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: The subsistence practice of using wild grasses was passed over generations in the Danube Gorges up to the first contacts with Neolithic farming groups.
source: Yet, it seems clear from our data that this specific subsistence practice was passed over generations in this regional context up to the first contacts of these foragers with Neolithic, farming groups in the second half of the seventh millennium BC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal distribution of evidence.

claim: The introduction of domesticated cereals from southwestern Asia was preceded by several millennia of collecting and consumption of native grass grains.
source: Previously, we suggested that some sort of exchange between LM foragers and first Neolithic groups in the southern Balkans might have allowed for the introduction of the domesticated species of Triticeae in the Danube Gorges area ∼6500 cal BC (Cristiani et al., 2016). Now, our extended study seems to suggest that this introduction of domesticated cereals, that is more productive cereal strains, from southwestern Asia was preceded by several millennia of collecting and consumption of native grass grains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of evidence.

claim: Zvelebil, 2014 argues for a form of niche constructing in temperate woodlands by means of deliberate forest clearance to increase productivity of nut and fruit trees, wetland plants, and possibly native grasses.
source: In a seminal synthesis about plant foods in the European Mesolithic, Zvelebil, 2014 reviews macro- and microbotanical, palynological, artifactual (antler hoes, mattocks, GST), and human osteological (dental size and presence of caries) evidence for the consumption of nuts and fruits by European Holocene foragers, arguing for a form of niche constructing in temperate woodlands by means of deliberate forest clearance in order 'to increase the productivity of nut and fruit trees and shrubs, wetland plants, and possibly native grasses' (Zvelebil, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a synthesis of European Mesolithic evidence.

claim: Zvelebil, 2014 emphasizes the existence of some form of husbandry of wild plant species, which did not necessarily lead to domestication.
source: The emphasis is on the existence of some form of husbandry of wild plant species, which did not necessarily lead to domestication.
evidence: This is a summary of Zvelebil's argument.

claim: There has been a recognition of the importance of plant foods in forager diets based on archaeological and ethnographic evidence.
source: For some time now, there has been a recognition of the importance of plant foods in forager diets, based on both archaeological and ethnographic evidence (Clarke, 1978; Lee et al., 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational literature.

claim: Research on mineralized dental plaque has significantly advanced awareness about ancient preagrarian food choices in Europe, Asia, and Africa.
source: Research on mineralized dental plaque has significantly advanced our awareness about ancient preagrarian food choices in Europe, Asia, and Africa, thanks to the dental plaque's potential to preserve plant microremains (Buckley et al., 2014; Cristiani et al., 2018; Cristiani et al., 2016; Cummings et al., 2016; Nava et al., 2021; Norström et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research on dental calculus.

claim: Wild cereals were found at the Epipaleolithic site of Ohalo II in Israel, dating to 23 kya.
source: In exceptional cases, good preservation has allowed for the remains of plant macroremains to be found, such as wild cereals at the Epipaleolithic site of Ohalo II in Israel, dating to 23 kya (Nadel et al., 2015; Piperno et al., 2004), or parenchyma remains at the Gravettian site of Dolní Věstonice in the Czech Republic (Pryor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to archaeological studies.

claim: Microremains of oat caryopses have been detected on ground stone tools found at the Gravettian site of Paglicci cave in Italy.
source: On the other hand, microremains of oat caryopses have been detected on GST found at the Gravettian site of Paglicci cave in Italy (Mariotti Lippi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an archaeological study.
